extracted.intended_audience: literate coffee-house readers / readers of The Tatler / Spectator; general 18th-century educated public interested in news, theatre, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Short-form periodical essays and coffee-house news items that include literary and theatrical criticism, commentary on translation and rhetoric, and reports of current events. The page mixes news dispatches with critical remarks about plays, acting, translation choices, and leadership rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of epithets/titles in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: "the poet has therefore wisely dropped them both for Dux Trojanus" (referring to avoiding awkward epithets like Pius Æneas and Pater Æneas)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer epithets/titles that fit the tone and avoid burlesque or absurdity; repeat consistent and appropriate epithets in speeches and narration. The example argues for replacing incongruous Latin honorifics with a more neutral, fitting epithet (Dux Trojanus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character actions with moral attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: "a loose action might be consistent enough with the usual manners of a soldier, though it became neither the chastity of a pious man, nor the gravity of the father of a people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying characters (in poetry, drama, or narrative), ensure actions align with their established moral attributes and social roles. An action may be plausible in one social role (soldier) but inappropriate for another (pious man, solemn father), so writers/translators should avoid incongruities that undermine character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer theatre that presents noble characters to reform taste
rubrics_metrics.description: "The amendment of these low gratifications is only to be made by people of condition, by encouraging the presentation of the noble characters drawn by Shakespeare and others"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and encourage plays that represent honourable, noble characters (Shakespearean models) rather than low comedy; doing so will cultivate polite and moral behaviour among the audience and society at large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of theatrical representation (actor+poet) to move audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a thing painted or related can irresistibly enter our hearts, what may not be performed by an excellent poet, when the character he draws is presented by the person, the manner, the look, and the motion, of an accomplished player?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective theatre depends on the combination of strong writing and accomplished acting: the poet's character plus the actor's person, manner, look, and motion can produce powerful emotional effects on the audience. Emphasize holistic coordination of text and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting naturalism and propriety suited to the role
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise of Mr. Bullock: "he has a peculiar talent of looking like a fool, and therefore excellently well qualified"; his "natural air and propriety of folly" and his manner of bearing a beating with "such a natural air and propriety of folly" are commended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors should embody roles with naturalness and appropriate mannerisms; successful low or comic parts require a convincing, proper representation of folly or vice. Physical comedy/violence should be rendered with an air of truth to delight the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should justly represent low life with humour and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: "The whole comedy is very just, and the low part of human life represented with much humour and wit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting low or vulgar aspects of life on stage, the representation should be 'just' (reasonable, truthful) and infused with humour and wit rather than mere coarseness, so as to entertain without degrading taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid historical/visual detail to produce emotional impact
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a thing painted or related can irresistibly enter our hearts... You have in that one sentence, a lively impression of his whole life and actions" (example comparing Le Brun's painting of Porus and Sallust's account of Catiline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concise, vivid description (either visual or verbal) that captures key details and causes/consequences to create a powerful, immediate impression of character and action; such economy of depiction can evoke strong pity, horror, or admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric of leadership: inspire rather than rely on bravado
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of Alexander and Caesar: Alexander's extravagant threat risked failure; Caesar "shows his men the unreasonableness of their fears in an obliging manner" and relies on praise of a trusted legion to secure cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective leadership speeches should not depend on reckless boasts or ultimatums; instead, reason with troops, address fears obligingly, and appeal to loyalty and honour (praise/selective delegation) to motivate and avoid risking morale through dangerous bravado.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and scene partners enhance actor performance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Skilful actors think it a very peculiar happiness to play in a scene with such as top their parts... those excellent players seem to be in their most shining circumstances" (on pairing actors like Bullock and Pinkethman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting and the pairing of actors matter: actors perform best when matched with scene partners who complement or 'top' their parts. Playwrights and directors should consider actor interplay when staging for maximal comic or tragic effect.
